newsitem.title: UK: Teenage smokers show early signs of addiction.
newsitem.headline: Teenage smokers show early signs of addiction.

text.p: Teenagers who smoke regularly light up right after they get up in the morning, which indicates they are already addicted, a survey published on Thursday found.
Only one in 14 teenager smokers can wait two hours before having their first cigarette of the day, the MORI survey of British children aged 11 to 16 found.
More than 40 percent of those surveyed thought tobacco should be classified as a "hard" drug like heroin.

The survey, commissioned by the Cancer Research Campaign charity, the British Medical Association, other cancer charities and anti-smoking group Action on Smoking and Health (ASH), found that one in 12 teenagers lit up withing five minutes of waking.

"We know from studies of adult smokers that the time before the first cigarette of the day is a strong indicator of tobacco dependence," said Martin Jarvis, a board member of ASH and senior scientist at the Imperial Cancer Research Fund.

"The fact that teenagers start smoking so early in the day is a clear indication that they are addicted. Nicotine is a powerful drug which keeps people hooked on smoking despite the fact that most smokers want to give up the habit."

ASH called for stricter regulation of tobacco in Britain. "It is scandalous that the industry is allowed to openly promote its addictive and dangerous products to young people," said ASH's chief executive Pamela Furness.
"For the past 30 years the tobacco companies have hidden the truth about nicotine and failed to warn smokers about the addictiveness of ther products."
Last month U.S. President Bill Clinton announced strict rules to control tobacco sales and advertising.
He strengthened the powers of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), requiring young people to provide a photo identification to prove they are the legal age of 18 before they could buy cigarettes.
The White House said an estimated 4.5 million children and adolescents smoke in the United States, with an estimated 3,000 starting each day.
A British survey found that, in 1994, 26 percent of boys and 30 percent of girls aged 15 were regular smokers, smoking more than 20 cigarettes a week.
